props.title: Force: Five

sections.content: **Force: Five (1981)** (1981) emerges from the explosion of American martial arts films in the early 1980s, riding the wave created by **Enter the Dragon** (1973). Director Robert Clouse, who also helmed Enter the Dragon, brings his signature style of combining martial arts spectacle with cult exploitation elements. The film follows an elite team of fighters infiltrating a religious cult's island compound, clearly influenced by the real-world Jonestown tragedy of 1978. Joe Lewis, a legitimate karate champion, leads the cast in what became one of the more distinctive entries in the "team of specialists" subgenre that flourished after **The Dirty Dozen** (1967).

sections.content: The martial arts choreography in Force: Five showcases the transition period between traditional karate-based fighting styles and the more dynamic Hong Kong-influenced techniques that would later dominate action cinema. The film's ensemble cast includes legitimate martial artists like Bong Soo Han and Richard Norton, following the template established by Game of Death (1978) where real fighting champions were featured prominently. This approach of casting actual martial artists would influence later films like **Bloodsport** (1988) and **American Ninja** (1985). SUBHEAD: Cult Cinema and Exploitation Elements

Force: Five's unusual blend of martial arts and cult infiltration narrative reflects the exploitation cinema trends of its era. Similar themes appear in **Kill and Kill Again** (1981) and **The Miami Connection** (1987), where martial arts heroes battle pseudo-religious organizations. These films often mixed genuine fighting talent with B-movie plot elements, creating a distinct subgenre that flourished in the direct-to-video market of the 1980s.
